'''''Coleus amboinicus''''' is a species of semi-[[Succulent plant|succulent]] [[perennial plant]] in the family ''[[Lamiaceae]]''.<ref name=POWO>{{cite web |url= https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:445902-1 |title= Coleus amboinicus Lour. |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=n.d. |website=Plants of the World Online |publisher=The Trustees of the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew |access-date=July 11, 2025}}</ref><ref name=COL>{{cite web |url= https://www.catalogueoflife.org/data/taxon/X22L |title= Coleus amboinicus Lour. |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=n.d. |website=Catalogue of Life |publisher=Species 2000 |access-date=July 11, 2025}}</ref><ref name="cabi">{{cite web|title=''Plectranthus amboinicus'' (Indian borage), Datasheet, Invasive Species Compendium|url=http://www.cabi.org/isc/datasheet/119834#tab1-nav|publisher=Centre for Agriculture and Biosciences International|date=23 November 2017|access-date=13 March 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170724072702/http://www.cabi.org/isc/datasheet/119834|archive-date=24 July 2017|url-status=live}}</ref> It has a pungent [[oregano]]-like flavor and odor. ''Coleus amboinicus'' is considered to be native to parts of Africa, the Arabian Peninsula, and India,<ref name="POWO_445902-1">{{cite web |title=''Coleus amboinicus'' Lour. |work=Plants of the World Online |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew|url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:445902-1 |access-date=2021-08-30 }}</ref> although it is widely cultivated and naturalized elsewhere in the tropics where it is used as a spice and ornamental plant.<ref name=cabi/> Common names in English include '''Indian borage''', '''country borage''', '''French thyme''', '''Indian mint''', '''Mexican mint''', '''Cuban oregano''', '''broad leaf thyme''', '''soup mint''', '''Spanish thyme'''.<ref name=cabi/> 

The species epithet, ''amboinicus'' refers to [[Ambon Island]], in Indonesia. In 1747, 45 years after his death, a volume written by [[Georg Eberhard Rumphius]] was published, including the plants he called ''Marrubium album Amboinicum'', with the local name ''Daun hati hati''. He had encountered them in Ambon and the [[Banda Islands]], both cultivated in gardens and growing wild.<ref name="Rumpf">{{cite book |last1=Rumphius |first1=Georg Eberhard |title=Herbarium amboinense Part 5 |date=1747 |location=Amsterdam |pages=294-295 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/10355#page/402/mode/1up |access-date=27 July 2025}}</ref> In 1790, the [[Linnean taxonomy|Linnaean]] name ''Coleus amboinicus'' was published by [[João de Loureiro]] (1717–1791) who had encountered the plants in [[Cochinchina]] and parts of India.<ref name="Loureiro">{{cite book |last1=de Loureiro |first1=João |title=Flora Cochinchinensis Volume 2 |date=1790 |location=Lisbon |page=372 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/89541#page/26/mode/1up |access-date=27 July 2025}}</ref>

== Description ==
A member of the mint family Lamiaceae,<ref name=cabi/> ''Coleus amboinicus'' grows up to {{convert|1|m|ft|abbr=on}} tall. The stem is fleshy, about {{convert|30-90|cm|abbr=on}}, either with long rigid hairs (hispidly villous) or densely covered with soft, short and erect hairs (tomentose). Old stems are smooth (glabrescent).

Leaves are {{convert|5-7|cm|abbr=on}} by {{convert|4-6|cm|abbr=on}}, fleshy, undivided (simple), broad, egg/oval-shaped with a tapering tip (ovate). The margins are coarsely crenate to dentate-crenate except in the base. They are thickly studded with hairs (pubescent), with the lower surface possessing the most numerous glandular hairs, giving a frosted appearance. The petiole is {{convert|2-4.5|cm|abbr=on}}. The aroma of the leaves can be described as a pungent combination of the aromas of oregano, [[thyme]], and [[turpentine]].<ref name="Ernest Small 1997, p. 488">''Culinary herbs'', by Ernest Small, National Research Council of Canada NRC Research Press, 1997, p. 488.</ref> The taste of the leaves is described as being similar to the one of oregano, but with a sharp mint-like flavor.<ref>''Florida's Best Herbs and Spices: Native and Exotic Plants Grown for Scent and Flavor'', by Charles R. Boning, Pineapple Press Inc, 2010 p. [https://books.google.com/books?id=uTIoxgzULJcC&dq=cuban+oregano&pg=PA75 75].</ref>

Flowers are on a short stem (shortly pedicelled), pale purplish, in dense 10-20 (or more) flowered dense whorls (cymes), at distant intervals, in a long slender spike-like raceme. Rachis {{convert|10-20|cm|abbr=on}}, fleshy and pubescent. The bracts are broadly ovate, {{convert|3-4|cm|abbr=on}} long, acute. The calyx is campanulate, {{convert|2-4|mm|abbr=on}} long, hirsute and glandular, subequally 5-toothed, upper tooth broadly ovate-oblong, obtuse, abruptly acute, lateral and lower teeth acute. Corolla blue, curved and declinate, {{convert|8-12|mm|abbr=on}} long, tube {{convert|3-4|mm|abbr=on}} long. Trumpet-like widened; limb 2-lipped, upper lip short, erect, puberulent, lower lip long, concave. Filaments are fused below into a tube around the style.

The seeds (nutlets) are smooth, pale-brown, roundish flattened, c. {{convert|0.7|by|0.5|mm|abbr=on}}.<ref>''Flora Malesiana'', Vol. 8, by Steenis, C. G. G. J. van (Cornelis Gijsbert Gerrit Jan); Steenis-Kruseman, M. J. van; Indonesia. Department Pertanian; Lembaga Ilmu Pengetahuan Indonesia; Kebun Raya Indonesia,  Publication date 1950, p. 387. Available on https://archive.org/details/floramalesiana83stee.</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
''Coleus amboinicus'' is native to [[Southern Africa|Southern]] and [[East Africa|Eastern Africa]], (from [[South Africa]] ([[KwaZulu-Natal]]) and [[Eswatini]] to [[Angola]] and [[Mozambique]] and north to [[Kenya]] and [[Tanzania]]) the Arabian Peninsula and India, where it grows in woodland or coastal bush, on rocky slopes and loamy or sandy flats at low elevations.<ref name="biodiversitylibrary.org">Codd, L. E. W.  et al. ''Flora of Southern Africa : the Republic of South Africa, Basutoland, Swaziland and South West Africa''. Vol. 28, part 4, 1981, page 148. Available on Biodiversity Heritage Library at https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/51375271.</ref><ref>''Flora Malesiana'', Vol. 8, by Steenis, C. G. G. J. van (Cornelis Gijsbert Gerrit Jan); Steenis-Kruseman, M. J. van; Indonesia. Departemen Pertanian; Lembaga Ilmu Pengetahuan Indonesia; Kebun Raya Indonesia,  Publication date 1950, p. 387. Available on https://archive.org/details/floramalesiana83stee.</ref><ref name=GRIN>{{GRIN | access-date = 21 August 2012}}</ref> The plant was later brought to Europe, and then from Spain to the Americas, hence the name Spanish thyme.<ref name="biodiversitylibrary.org"/><ref name="books.google.lk">{{cite book|title=Ethnic Culinary Herbs: A Guide to Identification and Cultivation in Hawaii |page=88 |author=George Staples |author2=Michael S. Kristiansen|date=1999|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=jbsdYHEJiDIC&q=88|publisher=University of Hawaii Press|isbn=978-0-8248-2094-7}}</ref>

==Research==
In [[basic research]], the effects of the [[essential oil]] were tested with other plant essential oils for possible use as a [[mosquito]] repellant.<ref name=cabi/><ref>{{cite journal|pmid=28013374|year=2017|last2=Mathew|first2=N|title=Mosquito repellent activity of volatile oils from selected aromatic plants|journal=Parasitology Research|volume=116|issue=2|pages=821–825|doi=10.1007/s00436-016-5351-4|last1=Lalthazuali|s2cid=5158038}}</ref>

==Uses==
The leaves are strongly flavored.<ref name=GRIN /> The herb is used as a substitute for oregano to mask the strong odors and flavors of fish, mutton, and goat.<ref>''The Herbalist in the Kitchen'', by Gary Allen, University of Illinois Press, 2010, p. [https://books.google.com/books?id=Fniv9ShKmxcC&dq=cuban+oregano&pg=PA198 198]</ref> It may be batter-fried to make ''pakodas'' or rasam.{{cn|date=August 2024}} In the Caribbean, leaves are commonly used when seasoning meats for its pungent aroma.<ref name=cabi/>

Fresh leaves are used to scent laundry and hair.<ref name=cabi/> It is also grown as an ornamental plant.<ref name=cabi/>

[[File:Variegated Cuban Oregano (Plectranthus amboinicus 'Variegatus') 1.jpg|thumb|right|{{center|Variegated Cuban oregano (''Coleus amboinicus'' 'Variegatus')}}]]

==Phytochemicals==
The main chemical compounds found in the essential oil of ''Coleus amboinicus'' are [[carvacrol]] (28.65%), [[thymol]] (21.66%), [[Humulene|α-humulene]] (9.67%), [[undecanal]] (8.29%), [[Terpinene|γ-terpinene]] (7.76%), [[p-Cymene|''p''-cymene]] (6.46%), [[caryophyllene oxide]] (5.85%), [[Terpineol|α-terpineol]] (3.28%), and [[Selinene|β-selinene]] (2.01%).<ref>{{cite journal|pmid=20668876|year=2010|last1=Senthilkumar|first1=A|title=Chemical composition and larvicidal activity of the essential oil of Plectranthus amboinicus (Lour.) Spreng against Anopheles stephensi: A malarial vector mosquito|journal=Parasitology Research|volume=107|issue=5|pages=1275–8|last2=Venkatesalu|first2=V|doi=10.1007/s00436-010-1996-6|s2cid=6776822}}</ref> Another analysis obtained thymol (41.3%), carvacrol (13.25%), [[Eucalyptol|1,8-cineole]] (5.45%), [[eugenol]] (4.40%), [[caryophyllene]] (4.20%), [[terpinolene]] (3.75%), [[α-pinene]] (3.20%), [[β-pinene]] (2.50%), [[methyl eugenol]] (2.10%), and [[β-phellandrene]] (1.90%). The variations can be attributed to the methodology used in the extraction process, seasonal variations, soil type, climate, genetic and geographical variations of the plant.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lopes |first1=P. Q |last2=Carneiro |first2=F. B |last3=De Sousa |first3=A. L |last4=Santos |first4=S. G |last5=Oliveira |first5=E. E |last6=Soares |first6=L. A |year=2017 |title=Technological Evaluation of Emulsions Containing the Volatile Oil from Leaves of Plectranthus Amboinicus Lour |url=https://phcog.com/article/view/13/49/159-167 |journal=Pharmacognosy Magazine |volume=13 |issue=49 |pages=159–167 |doi=10.4103/0973-1296.197646 |doi-broken-date=11 July 2025 |pmc=5307902 |pmid=28216901 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

== Cultivation ==
''Coleus amboinicus'' is a fast-growing plant commonly grown in gardens and indoors in pots. Propagation is by stem cuttings, but it can also be grown from seeds. In dry climates the herb grows easily in a well-drained, semi-shaded position. It is frost tender ([[Hardiness zone|USDA hardiness zones]] 10–11)<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.finegardening.com/plantguide/plectranthus-amboinicus-mexican-mint.aspx|title=Plectranthus amboinicus|website=Fine Gardening|access-date=2017-07-18}}</ref> and grows well in subtropical and tropical locations, but will do well in cooler climates if grown in a pot and brought indoors, or moved to a warm, sheltered position in winter. In Hawaii and other humid tropical locations, the plant requires full sun.<ref name="Ernest Small 1997, p. 488"/> It can be harvested throughout the growing season to be used fresh, dried, or frozen.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Cuban Oregano (Plectranthus amboinicus) {{!}} My Garden Life|url=https://www.mygardenlife.com/plant-library/2872/plectranthus/amboinicus|access-date=2022-02-08|website=www.mygardenlife.com}}</ref>
